claims.text: The initial CoCrFeMnNi alloy is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy has no pre-existing oxide films.
Plastic deformation in CoCrFeMnNi is mediated by dislocations.
Mechanical loading in an oxidizing and humid environment promotes formation of thin, brittle oxide films.
The environmentally generated oxide films form preferentially at high-stress regions, particularly crack tips.
Oxygen and water vapor interact with stressed regions of the alloy to form brittle oxide layers.
The oxide films disrupt dislocation motion and reduce local plasticity.
Oxide films act as sites for premature microcrack initiation and accelerated crack propagation.
Oxidizing and humid exposure causes earlier brittle fracture and a loss of toughness relative to inert-atmosphere loading.
Under inert conditions, CoCrFeMnNi exhibits ductile and tough baseline behavior without significant oxide formation.
Oxidizing and humid specimens will have lower fracture toughness, earlier crack initiation, and faster crack propagation than inert-atmosphere specimens.
XPS or AES will reveal thin, continuous oxide layers at crack-initiation sites.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate-to-high cyclic or static loads in oxygen- and moisture-rich service environments.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at extremely high temperature or under highly reducing conditions because oxidation kinetics and mechanisms differ.
Identical samples will be compared using tensile and impact tests in inert versus humid, oxygen-rich atmospheres.
Fracture toughness, absorbed energy, crack-initiation strain, crack-growth rate, and oxide characteristics will be measured.
The hypothesis is falsified if environmental exposure produces no significant mechanical degradation or if the proposed crack-tip oxide films are not detected.
Variations in oxide-film thickness and continuity could alter the degree of local embrittlement.
